title: An Old-House Owner’s Guide to New Technology
gist: A WIRED editor documents six months of retrofitting a 1907 Portland Craftsman with smart devices (Ecobee thermostat, Midea U-shaped window AC, Philips 4200 hub-free smart deadbolt, Toto S7A washlet, Feit and Zoiinet lighting, Whisker Litter-Robot 5 Pro, Sebo vacuums, OtO sprinkler, Kohler Aquifer faucet). The through-line is a purchase logic investors can generalize: in old housing stock, the winning products are the ones that let owners defer five-figure structural capex (rewiring, whole-home HVAC, in-ground irrigation) and that work with zero hub, zero electrician, and zero subscription. Aesthetics and unobtrusiveness, not feature count, are the binding constraint on adoption.

themes.theme: Retrofit-over-rewire: devices sold as capex deferral

insights.claim: In pre-war US housing stock, the highest-value smart-home products are the ones that let an owner postpone a structural renovation, not the ones with the most features — window AC units, plug-in overhead-light sockets and hose-fed sprinklers are all bought explicitly to delay whole-home HVAC, rewiring and in-ground irrigation.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: The addressable market for these categories is priced against a deferred contractor bill, not against a cheaper gadget — so gross margins can hold well above commodity-electronics levels.
insights.quote: At some point we will likely upgrade the air cooling system for the whole house, but these Midea units have made it possible to delay that choice without sacrificing comfort in our sleeping space.
insights.locator: A Smart Air Conditioner for Older Windows

insights.claim: Installing whole-home air conditioning in a 1907 house that had never had it was judged cost-prohibitive on day one, pushing the buyer to two Midea U-shaped window units instead — a substitution that costs roughly $400–$510 per unit versus a full system.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Window/portable AC is taking share from HVAC installs in the old-housing segment; watch unit-volume growth at Midea-type OEMs as a proxy for deferred HVAC capex.
insights.quote: Installing a proper whole-home air conditioning system into our home—which had never been done before—proved dauntingly cost-prohibitive as a day one update.
insights.locator: A Smart Air Conditioner for Older Windows

insights.claim: Midea's U-shaped window AC wins on a purely physical constraint of old buildings: it installs with the window open only about six inches versus roughly 20 inches for conventional window units, which matters because century-old sash windows often do not open fully.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: A mechanical form-factor moat beats app features in this category — competitors without the U-shape are structurally excluded from the old-housing installed base.
insights.quote: the unit’s U-shaped design makes it so you only have to have your window open around six inches to install, as opposed to the normal 20 inches of most traditional window air conditioners
insights.locator: A Smart Air Conditioner for Older Windows

insights.claim: A ~$22 Zoiinet Bluetooth remote-control light socket paired with a stick-on touch switch adds overhead lighting to a bedroom that only had wall mounts, entirely avoiding an electrician and any contact with the house's wiring.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Sub-$25 hardware substituting for a licensed-trade visit is the sharpest price-anchoring dynamic in smart home; the labor arbitrage, not the BOM, sets the willingness to pay.
insights.quote: rather than rewiring the room to add in overhead lighting (the bedrooms only came with wall mounts), we were able to install this socket without needing to hire an electrician

insights.claim: OtO's app-controlled smart sprinkler is differentiated from ordinary smart hose timers because it can set multiple watering zones from one placement, which an ecological landscape designer says is decisive for a garden still establishing itself.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Zoning capability without an in-ground system is the feature that lets OtO price at ~$499–$589 rather than at hose-timer economics.
insights.quote: A smart hose timer just runs one setting wherever you set the sprinkler down. OtO lets you set different zones from one spot, and that matters, because every part of a garden waters differently while it's establishing.
insights.locator: A Smart Sprinkler for the Yard

insights.claim: Lighting is presented as the single highest-leverage intervention for comfort in an inhabited space, explicitly tied to the work-from-home context, and was solved with ~$13–$16 Feit Electric smart bulbs retrofitted into vintage fixtures rather than any fixture replacement.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Smart bulbs remain the cheapest entry point into the ecosystem and the most common Alexa attach vector — volume leader even as ASPs stay in the low teens.
insights.quote: I’m convinced lighting is one of the most important things we can do to make inhabited environments more comfortable, especially if you’ll be working from home.

themes.theme: No hub, no subscription as the buying filter

insights.claim: The Philips 4200 fingerprint smart deadbolt was chosen over rival smart locks specifically because Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are built in, it runs on batteries, needs no hardwiring, and requires no hub, dongle or subscription — total cost about $120 all-in.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Recurring-revenue smart-home models are losing the mainstream purchase decision to hub-free one-time-purchase hardware; subscription attach rates in the lock category look structurally capped.
insights.quote: the Philips 4200 does not require its own “hub,” dongle, or additional apparatus in order to start working immediately
insights.locator: A Smart Lock That Doesn’t Require Hardwiring

insights.claim: Ecobee's Enhanced thermostat was selected over Google Nest because Nest lacks Ecobee's presence sensors, and Ecobee's radar-based motion detection plus larger touchscreen justified the midrange (~$188–$200) tier over the cheaper Essential model.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Sensor presence — not brand or ecosystem — is the swing feature in thermostat share; Google is losing informed buyers on a hardware gap, not on software.
insights.quote: which prioritizes the unit’s ease of setup and intuitive interface—this made a strong case for selecting the Ecobee over other similar smart thermostats, like the Google Nest, which lacks the Ecobee’s presence sensors

themes.theme: Utility rebates and resource specs subsidize the upgrade

insights.claim: Many US states run smart-thermostat rebate programs through local gas and power utilities, and this household is currently earning about $10 off each monthly bill simply for having one installed — a payback of roughly 20 months on a ~$200 device.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Utility demand-response budgets are effectively a hidden distribution channel and price subsidy for connected-thermostat OEMs; rebate rollbacks would hit unit economics directly.
insights.quote: Many states have a smart thermostat rebate program through local gas and power companies, and right now we’re earning around $10 off each monthly bill for having a smart thermostat in the house.

insights.claim: Toto's Aurora Washlet+ S7A with the Integravity System uses one gallon per flush against an EPA standard of 1.6 gallons, pairing luxury positioning ($2,554–$3,648) with a measurable water-efficiency claim.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Water-efficiency headroom below regulatory minimums is becoming a premium-fixture selling point — relevant as drought-state codes tighten.
insights.quote: It also only uses one gallon of water per flush, which is well below the Environmental Protection Agency standard of 1.6 gallons per flush.

insights.claim: The OtO sprinkler's built-in solar panel kept it running unplugged for an entire summer on a single initial charge, removing any electrical run to the yard.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Onboard solar is what makes untethered outdoor smart hardware viable; expect it to become table stakes across yard-tech SKUs.
insights.quote: the OtO’s built-in solar panel is great—we’ve left it unplugged all summer after a single full charge to get things started
insights.locator: A Smart Sprinkler for the Yard

themes.theme: Aesthetics as the binding adoption constraint

insights.claim: The author's stated test for good smart-home tech is that it be subtle, effective and unobtrusive — invisibility, not capability, is what makes a connected device acceptable in a historic-registry home.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Industrial design and disappearing form factors are the real competitive axis in mature smart-home categories; feature-stacking without design loses the premium buyer.
insights.quote: To me, this is emblematic smart-home tech: subtle, effective, and unobtrusive.
insights.locator: A Smart Lock That Doesn’t Require Hardwiring

insights.claim: Sebo's retro-styled German upright vacuums ($799–$1,149) are bought partly because they are attractive enough to leave out in the open, inverting the usual out-of-sight appliance logic and solving a real constraint in old homes where closet space is scarce.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: A design premium of 3–5x commodity vacuum pricing is sustainable when the product doubles as decor — the same playbook that repriced small kitchen appliances.
insights.quote: these are vacuum cleaners so attractive you’ll feel bad about sticking them in your closet

insights.claim: The buyer knowingly accepted an aesthetic mismatch on the $2,554+ Toto washlet — conceding it looks nothing like 1907 — because the functional gain outweighed period authenticity, showing that vintage-home owners will break their own design rules for a high-enough utility payoff.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Bathroom tech has crossed the utility threshold where design objections stop blocking purchase — bullish for premium washlet penetration in the US.
insights.quote: Does the Toto S7A “look vintage” in any way? No. Frankly, I think a person in 1907 would be positively astonished by the experience of using this technology

insights.claim: Whisker's $899 Litter-Robot 5 Pro is valued less for automation than for odor control that distinguishes between waste types and for physically disappearing into a laundry-room corner, plus app data confirming the pet's routine health behavior.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Pet-tech at $899 sells on sensory outcomes and health telemetry, not labor savings — a durable premium tier inside an otherwise commoditized pet-supplies market.
insights.quote: the most important aesthetic consideration around why we like the LR5 is its relative unobtrusiveness: It disappears into the corner of our laundry room

insights.claim: Kohler's $3,375 Aquifer 4-in-1 beverage faucet — filtered, hot and sparkling water with a refillable CO2 cartridge — is displacing packaged sparkling water purchases in this household, with the author explicitly noting savings on restocking La Croix.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: At-tap carbonation moves from countertop appliance to permanent plumbing fixture — a slow structural headwind for canned sparkling-water volumes in affluent households.
insights.quote: the sparkling water attachment is already saving me money on restocking La Croix

insights.claim: Nearly every purchase in the piece is sourced to WIRED's own buying guides and named staff reviewers, with retailer links and an affiliate-compensation disclosure attached — the review franchise functions as the demand-generation layer for the commerce revenue.
insights.speaker: Jordan Michelman
insights.so_what: Editorial buying guides remain a high-intent funnel for retail affiliate revenue; treat this format as a media monetization proxy rather than independent product signal.
insights.quote: we consulted WIRED’s guide to smart sprinklers and went with reviewer Christopher Null’s qualified recommendation around OtO
insights.locator: A Smart Sprinkler for the Yard
